title: Feeding, food safety and measuring change in the field

say: Feeding, food safety and measuring change.
This is the video for module two of Community Nutrition and Food Security.
If you can only change one thing in your community, change how babies and young children are fed. WHO and UNICEF guidance is clear and simple.

panel.heading: If you change one thing
items: Feed babies and young children well
Keep food safe from farm to plate
Measure, record and refer early

say: This module gives you three practical tools: feeding the first 1,000 days, keeping food safe, and simple measures of progress.

say: Put the baby to the breast within one hour of birth. The first thick yellow milk, colostrum, is rich in antibodies. Do not throw it away.

panel.heading: Breast milk first, breast milk only
items: Breastfeed within one hour of birth
Keep the colostrum, do not throw it away
Only breast milk for six months
Feed on demand, day and night
Continue up to two years or beyond

say: Give only breast milk for the first six months. No water, herbal drinks or pap, unless a health worker advises it for a medical reason. Breast milk contains enough water even in hot weather.

panel.heading: Breast milk first, breast milk only

Only breast milk for six months
Feed on demand, day and night
Continue up to two years or beyond

say: Feed on demand, day and night, and continue breastfeeding up to two years or beyond while other foods are added.

say: At about six months, breast milk alone no longer covers a baby's needs for energy, iron and zinc. Start with thick porridge or well-mashed food.

panel.heading: First foods, step by step
items: 6 to 8 months: thick, mashed food
2 to 3 meals a day, plus breastfeeds
9 to 23 months: 3 to 4 meals
Add 1 to 2 snacks if hungry
Aim for 5 of 8 food groups

say: At 6 to 8 months, give 2 to 3 meals a day, starting with 2 to 3 tablespoons and slowly increasing.

panel.heading: First foods, step by step
items: 6 to 8 months: thick, mashed food
2 to 3 meals a day, plus breastfeeds
9 to 23 months: 3 to 4 meals
Add 1 to 2 snacks if hungry
Aim for 5 of 8 food groups

say: From 9 to 23 months, give 3 to 4 meals a day, with 1 to 2 nutritious snacks if the child is hungry.

panel.heading: First foods, step by step
items: 6 to 8 months: thick, mashed food
2 to 3 meals a day, plus breastfeeds
9 to 23 months: 3 to 4 meals
Add 1 to 2 snacks if hungry
Aim for 5 of 8 food groups

say: For variety, aim for at least 5 of the 8 food groups for young children. Plain pap covers only one group, so it must be enriched.

panel.heading: First foods, step by step
items: 6 to 8 months: thick, mashed food
2 to 3 meals a day, plus breastfeeds
9 to 23 months: 3 to 4 meals
Add 1 to 2 snacks if hungry
Aim for 5 of 8 food groups
panel.rule: Thick enough to stay on a tilted spoon, never a thin drink.

say: For example, Chiamaka in Owerri gave her 8-month-old daughter thin ogi with sugar, plus breast milk. That scores just 2 of 8 groups.
She made the ogi thicker and stirred in 1 tablespoon of smooth groundnut paste and 1 teaspoon of ground crayfish.
At lunch she mashed an egg into yam, and gave ripe pawpaw as a snack. She dropped the sugar. Now the baby eats from 6 of 8 groups, at a modest extra cost.
Keep baby food safe. Wash hands with soap before preparing food and before feeding. Use a clean cup and spoon, because a feeding bottle is hard to clean.

cards.d: Wash hands with soap. Use a clean cup and spoon, not a feeding bottle.
Grind groundnuts into smooth paste. Whole nuts can choke a young child.
No honey before the first birthday. No sweet drinks, tea or coffee. Feed fresh food.

say: Grind groundnuts into smooth paste, because whole nuts can choke a young child.

say: Do not give honey before the first birthday. Avoid sweet drinks, tea and coffee, and feed freshly made food, not food kept for hours.

say: Food that is contaminated or mouldy does not become good nutrition. Follow the five keys. Keep clean. Separate raw and cooked. Cook thoroughly. Keep food at safe temperatures. And use safe, boiled or treated water.
Dry grain and groundnuts well, and throw away mouldy ones. The poison in mould cannot be seen or cooked away.

panel.heading: The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
items: Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Use safe water and raw materials
Dry and sort grain; throw out mould

say: For example, Ruth in Ibadan cooked jollof rice and stew for a naming ceremony. It was ready at 1 pm, and guests left at 5 pm. She has no fridge.

panel.heading: Ruth and the 2-hour rule
items: Rice ready at 1 pm, guests gone at 5 pm
That is 4 hours: double the limit
She throws the rice away
Next time: stew hot, rice in batches

say: That is 4 hours at room temperature, double the 2-hour limit. Rice left warm can grow bacteria whose poisons reheating does not destroy.

panel.heading: Ruth and the 2-hour rule
items: Rice ready at 1 pm, guests gone at 5 pm
That is 4 hours: double the limit
She throws the rice away
Next time: stew hot, rice in batches

say: So she throws the rice away instead of risking diarrhoea in her children.

panel.heading: Ruth and the 2-hour rule
items: Rice ready at 1 pm, guests gone at 5 pm
That is 4 hours: double the limit
She throws the rice away
Next time: stew hot, rice in batches

say: Next time she will keep stew on a low fire, serve rice in batches, and take food to keep to her neighbour's fridge within 2 hours.

panel.heading: Ruth and the 2-hour rule
items: Rice ready at 1 pm, guests gone at 5 pm
That is 4 hours: double the limit

Next time: stew hot, rice in batches
panel.rule: Cooked food: no more than 2 hours at room temperature.

say: MUAC means mid-upper arm circumference, for children aged 6 to 59 months. Red means severe acute malnutrition. Refer the same day.
Also press both feet for 3 seconds. A dent left on both feet is oedema, which also means refer at once.

cards.d: Severe acute malnutrition. Refer to a health facility the same day.
Moderate acute malnutrition. Clinic assessment and feeding support.
Not acutely malnourished by MUAC. Keep feeding well; recheck monthly.

say: Yellow means moderate acute malnutrition. Fatima measured 18-month-old Sani at 118 mm, explained calmly, went with his mother to the clinic, and recorded a follow-up reading.

cards.d: Severe acute malnutrition. Refer to a health facility the same day.
Moderate acute malnutrition. Clinic assessment and feeding support.
Not acutely malnourished by MUAC. Keep feeding well; recheck monthly.

say: Green means keep feeding well and recheck monthly. Your role is to screen, record and refer. Never give medicines or therapeutic food yourself.

cards.d: Severe acute malnutrition. Refer to a health facility the same day.
Moderate acute malnutrition. Clinic assessment and feeding support.
Not acutely malnourished by MUAC. Keep feeding well; recheck monthly.

say: To remember. Breastfeed early and exclusively for six months, then add thick, enriched foods.
Keep cooked food out no more than 2 hours. Refer red MUAC or oedema the same day. And track your weekly diet score.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Breastfeed within one hour, only breast milk to six months
Thick, enriched first foods; 5 of 8 groups
No cooked food out more than 2 hours
Red MUAC or oedema: same-day referral
Track the weekly diet score and its average
